d.title: The k constant decides how much rank 1 dominates rank 2
d.caption: RRF scores a document as `1 / (k + rank)`, so **k sets how steeply the weight falls off.** At k=0 rank 1 is worth **twice** rank 2; at k=60 — the conventional default — the ratio is **1.016**, which is nearly flat. So the convention is a deliberate choice to treat the top ten or twenty positions as roughly equivalent, and **it only makes sense when every retriever's ranks are meaningful** — which 6.3 showed BM25's are not past rank 4 on this corpus.

d.title: Fusion made it worse, by a lot
d.caption: The expected result is that combining two retrievers beats either. **Dense alone scores 0.964 MRR on natural-language queries; RRF 1:1 scores 0.393** — worse than less than half of it. The cause is 6.3's finding: **BM25 produces 4 meaningful ranks and 37 ties**, and RRF reads ranks as evidence, so it is being handed 37 arbitrary votes per query and treating them as opinions. **Fusion is only as good as the worst ranking it trusts.**

d.title: No weight fixes it, because the two classes want opposite weights
d.caption: Sweeping the weight does not find a setting that works — **it finds that the two query classes want opposite ends of the range.** Natural-language queries improve monotonically toward dense-only, reaching **0.964 at 1:0**. Exact-term queries are **perfect at 1:1 and degrade to 0.844 at 10:1.** There is no single weight that serves both, which means the choice is **a decision about which query class to favour** rather than a tuning problem with a solution.

d.title: The formula penalises a candidate for resembling what is already chosen
d.caption: Two terms with one dial. **λ times similarity to the query, minus (1−λ) times the maximum similarity to anything already selected** — so a document competes on relevance and is docked for redundancy against the set so far. At **λ = 1** it is plain relevance ranking and MMR does nothing. At **λ = 0** it ignores the query entirely and maximises diversity, which is useless. The useful range is in between, and §03 measures what that costs on the metrics.

nodes.label: Selection is greedy and sequential
nodes.sub: which is why it needs fetch_k

d.title: The metric can move and cannot move in the direction of the benefit
d.caption: λ from 1.0 to 0.3 and the metrics **only get worse**: MRR 0.964 to 0.929, recall 1.000 to 0.893. Worth separating from 5.8's ceiling problem, which it resembles. **There, P@5 could not move because of the label counts. Here the metric *can* move — it moves downward — but it cannot move in the direction of the benefit, because the benefit is not a ranking property.** Four slots of distinct cancellation procedures beat four of the same one, and no ranking metric expresses that.

d.title: fetch_k is what makes diversity possible at all
d.caption: MMR selects greedily **from the candidates it was given**, so with `fetch_k = k` there is nothing to choose between — it returns the same five documents in a different order. Widening the pool is what lets it reach past the near-duplicates: at `fetch_k=5` the result is **five cancellation documents**; at 10 it has pulled in `api-versioning` and `bill-seats`. Which is the `fetch_k > k` rule arriving for the second time, and 6.7 is the third.

d.title: Stage one had to fetch 20 for the document to be present at all
d.caption: The case reranking exists for, and the detail that makes it work. **The relevant document was outside the top 5, so nothing could have promoted it if `fetch_k` had been 5** — a reranker reorders candidates and cannot conjure one. Which is the two-stage design working exactly as 5.1 described, and **the `fetch_k > k` rule arriving for the third time**: 5.1 derived it, 6.6 needed it for diversity, and here it is a precondition for reranking to help.

d.title: Reranking makes one class perfect and the other worse
d.caption: **Exact-term queries go from 0.781 MRR to a perfect 1.000, and natural-language queries go from 0.964 down to 0.845.** So reranking is not an improvement — it is **a trade between query classes**, exactly like 6.5's weight sweep, and reported as a single average it would read as a small gain and hide both effects. Which is the reason 6.9 insists on reporting per class: an aggregate here would be the least informative number available.

d.title: Where it goes wrong: the reranker demotes correct answers
d.caption: Three natural-language queries where dense had the right document at rank 1 and **the reranker pushed it down** — one to rank 3, one to **rank 11**. The cross-encoder is more accurate on average and **its errors are not the same errors**, so swapping it in trades dense's failures for its own. Which is why §05's candidate-count dial matters: more candidates gives the reranker more room to be right **and more room to be wrong.**

d.title: Accuracy stops at 20 and latency does not
d.caption: **Exact-term MRR reaches 1.000 at `fetch=20` and stays there at 41, while latency goes from 1.479 s to 2.308 s** — so the last 21 candidates are pure cost. Latency grows roughly linearly, because **the cross-encoder scores every pair** — 6.1's per-document cost, now with a knob on it. And natural-language MRR is flat at 0.845 from 10 onward, so nothing in this sweep argues for going past 20.

d.title: Four narrowings, and the arithmetic matters more than any accuracy figure
d.caption: **That ordering is 5.1's principle applied four times: never let an expensive stage see more documents than it must.** 41 documents enter, fusion keeps 20, diversification narrows to 8, reranking scores those 8 and returns 5. And the claim at the end of the lesson is that **the arithmetic of that narrowing turns out to matter more than any accuracy figure in the lesson** — which §03 demonstrates by making the pipeline *faster* by adding a stage to it.

d.title: Adding a stage made the pipeline faster
d.caption: `dense + rerank` cross-encodes **20** candidates. The full pipeline inserts MMR, which **narrows those 20 to 8 before the reranker runs** — so the expensive stage does **8 forward passes instead of 20**. At 6.1's measured ~68 ms per pair that is a saving of roughly **0.8 s**, and MMR itself is a handful of dot products over 20 vectors. Which is the counter-intuitive result worth keeping: **a stage that filters before an expensive stage can pay for itself in latency alone**, independently of whether it improves anything.

nodes.label: A filter can pay in latency alone

d.title: Three stages, three different verdicts
d.caption: **Not every stage pays for itself, and the ablation is the only way to know which.** One stage is pure cost, one helps a class and harms another, and one improves **both latency and accuracy — for reasons unrelated to the diversity it was designed for.** And what the table cannot show is answer quality, which is what the diversity was for in the first place. Both limitations point the same way: **a pipeline measured only on ranking metrics is a pipeline whose stages you partly do not understand.**

d.title: A stage's value is a property of the pipeline, not of the stage
d.caption: Step four is what this lesson adds to the usual method. **`hybrid` genuinely helped before reranking existed and contributed nothing after** — so you cannot evaluate a technique in isolation and carry the result forward. **A stage's value is not a property of the stage; it is a property of the pipeline it sits in.** Which gives the closing line its force: **a pipeline assembled from a blog post is a pipeline nobody has ablated.**

d.title: One query, four metrics, computed by hand
d.caption: Two relevant documents, both retrieved, both at the top: the hit pattern is `[1, 1, 0, 0, 0]`. **Recall@5 is 1.000 because both were found. P@5 is 0.400 because three of five slots are not relevant — and cannot be, since only two relevant documents exist.** MRR is 1.000 from the first hit, and NDCG weights by position, so a perfect ordering of an imperfect slate still scores below 1. **Three of the four numbers are about the slate size rather than the retriever.**

state: the slate size, not the retriever

d.title: The maximum achievable mean P@5 on this set is 0.214
d.caption: **13 of 14 queries have exactly one relevant document**, so for those the best possible P@5 is **1/5 = 0.200** — and the mean ceiling across the set is **0.214.** Any P@5 you measure here is being compared against that, not against 1.0. **The remedy is to change the measurement rather than chase the number**: evaluate at `k=1`, where the ceiling is 1.0, or build a label set with graded relevance so several documents can be partially correct. **Both are label-side changes, which is the tell that the problem was never in the retriever.**

d.title: Symptom to fix, and the row where every number looks healthy
d.caption: **The third row is the one easiest to miss, because every number looks healthy.** 6.6's near-duplicate case is exactly that: perfect MRR with a context window full of four cancellation procedures for four different situations. **Ranking metrics score the ranking, not the context.** And the fourth row is this lesson's own warning — a low P@k with few relevant documents is probably at ceiling, so **check before acting.**

d.title: No retriever dominates, which is the module's conclusion
d.caption: Read across: **dense wins every natural-language column and loses both exact-term columns; BM25 does the exact reverse, at 1.000 on both exact-term metrics and 0.286 MRR on natural language.** And RRF, which exists to resolve this, lands at **0.393 natural MRR — worse than dense alone.** So the module's conclusion is not a recommendation: **there is no configuration that is best, and the choice is a statement about which query class your users actually send.**
